claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys are governed by grain-boundary chemistry.
Targeted dopants that segregate beneficially at grain boundaries enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
Targeted grain-boundary dopants beneficially modulate dislocation/grain-boundary interactions.
The comparison should use a baseline alloy with conventional grain-boundary chemistry and a controlled, reproducible microstructure.
The added dopants can be made to segregate selectively to grain boundaries without causing bulk phase changes.
The temperature range 800–1200 °C is relevant for the proposed high-temperature comparison.
Grain size and processing history should be held similar between doped and undoped samples.
Dopant segregation produces a modified grain-boundary composition.
The modified grain-boundary composition strengthens intergranular bonds.
The modified grain-boundary composition alters dislocation nucleation and motion at grain boundaries.
Dopant-induced segregation reduces grain-boundary sliding.
Dopant-induced segregation reduces intergranular cavitation.
Altered dislocation interactions at doped grain boundaries improve strain hardening.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion and altered dislocation interactions delay crack initiation.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the doped alloy will have greater high-temperature toughness.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the doped alloy will sustain or increase high-temperature plastic strain.
The predicted improvement will be manifested as higher yield strength, extended ductility, and reduced intergranular cracking.
The effect is expected only for comparable microstructures in the 800–1200 °C range and may change outside that range or when secondary phases form.
High-temperature oxidation could complicate the measured plasticity and toughness effects.
Failure to observe statistically significant mechanical improvement, or failure to produce a measurable grain-boundary chemistry change, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires successful grain-boundary segregation, but the falsification rule treats absence of a measurable chemistry change as falsification. That outcome would instead show failure to realize the intervention and would not decisively test its proposed causal effect.
